## **Motivation**

Upon entering university, students’ social networks become far more complex. With classmates from different courses, peers from CCAs, acquaintances from forums or events, and neighbors in student residences, it becomes hard to memorize all of these relations and information about them due to the sheer number of connections. We want an all-in-one software that can manage this network for us, only requiring minimal interaction.

The need for memo management and learning management grows as we enter university, and many sudden thoughts of plans, received tasks, and ideation inspirational moments are common, and there may be various connections between this information, which existing note-taking software and Personal Knowledge Management Software do not put much emphasis on.

While digital mind map applications (like ClickUp, Miro, MindMup, Edrawsoft) exist, they are not well-equipped to handle the complexity of detailed character webs.

## **Aim**

Developed a Personal Knowledge Management Software focusing on managing personal fragmented information from a logical and relational perspective.

* We hope to achieve fast information input and retrieval, visualization, multi-format data export, and sharing with an optimized front-end that supports fuzzy search, autocomplete, and filtering.  
* We hope to enable the inference and querying of logical relationships within complex object-property-relation networks, utilizing existing logical programming frameworks like the Prolog Language.  
* In the long run, we hope to build an open platform that allows other developers to perform secondary development with respect to the front-end under a unified database infrastructure, cultivating a platform ecosystem focusing on managing fragmented information.

## **User Scenarios**

* Reader: As a reader who wants to understand and track complex character relationships, I want to be able to:  
  * Organize and visualize character relationships in a clear and dynamic mind map.  
  * Record the first appearance of each character by page number for quick reference.  
  * Document character attributes (e.g., age, personality, role in the story).  
  * Track the connections between characters and the plot, helping to follow story arcs easily.  
* Stock Analyst: As a stock analyst who wants to track and analyze market data and relationships, I want to be able to:  
  * Record and visualize connections between market trends, global news, and financial instruments (e.g., stocks, funds, commodities, cryptocurrencies).  
  * Track price movements over time and how they correlate with external events.  
  * Organize complex interdependencies between assets and generate insights from data patterns.  
* President of the Student Union: As a Student Union president who wants to manage people, tasks, and event progress, I want to be able to:  
  * Organize task ownership by mapping team members to their responsibilities.  
  * Track event progress in real-time, including deadlines and key milestones.  
  * Document meeting schedules, related issues, and action items for quick reference and follow-up.  
* Class Head Teacher (Secondary School): As a class head teacher who wants to monitor student performance and communicate with parents, I want to be able to:  
  * Record and track students' daily academic progress for personalized feedback.  
  * Document parent feedback and concerns systematically.  
  * Visualize student-teacher-parent interactions and monitor engagement levels.  
* Vlogger / Content Creator: As a vlogger or content creator who wants to organize ideas and moments for storytelling, I want to be able to:  
  * Record daily experiences or travel details and categorize them by themes or storylines.  
  * Identify and connect disparate events to form coherent narratives for videos or articles.  
  * Easily retrieve previous ideas and captured moments during content creation.  
* Editor (Literary Reviewer): As an editor who wants to analyze and verify logical consistency, I want to be able to:  
  * Map out and review logical relationships across a manuscript.  
  * Identify plot inconsistencies or contradictions within the text.  
  * Document and track feedback points for easy communication with authors.

## **Architecture & Concepts**

### **Overview**

JotMind is a structured personal knowledge management application designed to help users record, visualize, and interlink fragmented information from daily life. The architecture revolves around a central *knowledge base*, partitioned into modular *knowledge clusters*, each rendered through customizable *views*. A *universal command interface* allows intuitive natural language interaction with the knowledge graph. JotMind aims to unify concepts from note-taking apps, relationship managers, and life trackers into one flexible, extensible system.

### **Knowledge Base**

* Each user has exactly one *Knowledge Base*, a private graph-like data space.  
* All information, including people, events, tools, and concepts, is stored as structured nodes and edges.

### **Knowledge Cluster**

* A *Knowledge Cluster* groups semantically similar nodes (e.g., People, Events, Concepts).  
* Each cluster follows a single *Cluster Template*, defining:  
  * Default views (e.g., network, timeline, table)  
  * Node/edge types and default properties  
  * Rendering rules and user interaction logic  
* All clusters are **singletons**; multiple clusters of the same type are not allowed to avoid redundant inter-cluster links. Instead, tags and filters allow intra-cluster segmentation.

### **Cluster Template**

* A *Cluster Template* describes how a cluster behaves and appears.  
* Contains both backend and frontend configurations:  
  * Backend: node/edge types, default properties, and LLM parsing schemas  
  * Frontend: rendering controllers, view layouts, component inheritance trees  
* Users cannot currently customize templates in-app. Developer APIs may support this in the future.

### **View System**

* Each *View* presents one cluster from a specific perspective.  
* Supported core views:  
  * **Cards View**: sequential arrangement of entries  
  * **Network View**: graphical layout for relationship-centric data  
  * **Timeline View**: sequential arrangement of time-based entries  
  * **Table View**: tabular browsing and bulk editing  
  * **Statistics View**: high-level metrics via charts/cards  
* Extended views include Kanban, Calendar, and Gantt charts.  
* Views render only one cluster at a time. Inter-cluster connections are visually de-emphasized but can be interacted with (e.g., jump links).  
* Views reuse visual components through a base component family (e.g., shared base classes for nodes, cards, and editors).

### **Static Nodes**

* *Static Nodes* are read-only predefined nodes (e.g., standard workout exercises or vocab entries).  
* They behave identically to regular nodes within singleton clusters.

### **Module System**

* A *Module* is a logical unit bundling multiple cluster templates, views, and plugins.  
* Example: A "Fitness Tracker" module contains templates for workout sessions and exercises.  
* Modules cannot have circular dependencies and are currently hardcoded. Future versions will support dynamic loading and publishing.

### **Universal Command Interface**

* Users can interact with the knowledge base via natural language.  
* Inputs are parsed by LLMs using RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) to generate structured JSON commands.  
* Commands follow a strict schema, e.g.:

| {  "type": "propertyIs",  "cluster": "People",  "key": "school",  "value": "Tsinghua University"} |
| :---- |

* Invalid or vague interpretations are discarded. Fallbacks include full-text search.  
* All parsed commands are displayed for user selection and confirmation.

### **Inter-Cluster Relationships**

* Nodes can reference nodes from other clusters (e.g., "Met John at ICRA 2025").  
* These connections are shown in detail views and enable cross-cluster navigation but are generally not visualized in the default view.

### **Search and Filtering**

* Both full-text and structured search are supported.  
* The scope (single cluster vs. entire base) is explicitly defined per command schema.  
* Filters (e.g., date range, tags, involved people) refine view outputs.

### **Onboarding and Progression**

* First-time users are guided through a tutorial with sample data.  
* Usage is progressively layered: beginner use focuses on basic views and input; advanced users can explore AI-assisted tracking, statistics, and plugin modules.

# **Security**

Security is a key focus in our application, as we manage sensitive user data and want to ensure both privacy and system integrity. Our current authentication is implemented entirely through Better Auth, providing a streamlined and secure login/sign-up process.

![][image4]![][image5]

## **1\) Purpose**

Enable users to register and log in securely without implementing custom token logic or password storage, leveraging Better Auth’s built-in security features.

## **2\) User Benefit**

Users can authenticate quickly without managing passwords, benefiting from Better Auth’s secure session handling and provider integration.

## **3\) Current Scope (Implemented)**

* Email-based sign-up and login handled via Better Auth.

* Built-in session management, CSRF protection, and cookie handling by Better Auth.

Planned: Integration with additional identity providers supported by Better Auth.

## **4\) How It Works**

1. User enters their email to sign up or log in.

2. Better Auth handles the authentication flow and creates a secure session.

3. User is redirected to the app with an active session.

## **5\) Error Handling**

* Invalid email → “Invalid email address”

* Unregistered email (login) → “Account not found”

* Backend/auth error → generic error modal with retry option

Error messages are standardized across the frontend and backend.

## **6\) Testing**

* Unit tests: Email validation and auth API request handling.

* Integration tests: End-to-end sign-up/login flow with Better Auth.

## **7\) Design Decisions**

* Selected Better Auth for its secure defaults, built-in provider support, and reduced custom auth code.

* Avoided building a custom token/JWT system to minimize complexity and attack surface.

* Unified login and signup into one flow for a consistent user experience.

### 

### **Verification of OTP (Intended to do)**

The correct OTP must be used within two minutes with no more than three attempts in order for verification to be successful. Otherwise, the requisite error message will be displayed and the user will need to resend their OTP or move to the previous page to correct their email (if it is wrong) and have another OTP generated.

| Frontend |  |
| :---: | ----- |
| Topic | Explanation |
| Design/ thought process | The OTP verification screen serves both login and sign-up purposes, depending on whether the entered email already exists in our system. To avoid asking existing users to re-verify their email, we’ve unified the flow. After OTP verification, the backend always returns a JWT token: If the email exists, the user receives a User Token and is logged in. If the email doesn’t exist, they receive an Email Token, which confirms their email is valid and is used to proceed with sign-up. Based on the type of token returned, the app redirects the user either to the home screen (for login) or the sign-up screen (for new users).  |
| Storing of JWT Tokens | Both the user and email JWT token is stored in a secured encrypted cache of the app (Using expo-secure-store). It is retrieved and added to the authentication header of every api called made by the client subsequently. |
| Error handling | There are 3 unique error messages than are handled specifically for OTPs: OTP is invalid OTP is expired OTP is over entered |

| Backend |  |
| :---: | ----- |
| Topic | Explanation |
| Verification of user by email | The OTP generated in the previous step is recorded against the user’s email. This is done for the following reasons: Discern between a new and a returning user  Prevent spamming of unauthorised emails into the main system. |
| Checking OTP validity | Checks validity of OTP is based on correctness, time entered and number of attempts. Most obviously, correctness is required so as to ensure that bad actors do not access the app. This is coupled with the limit set on the possible number of attempts to prevent bad actors from guessing the OTP. Finally, the time entered is also set so that OTP will expire and in the case of duplicates, it will not affect the security of the app. |
| Producing JWT token | As explained in the frontend table above, two different JWTs will be generated depending if the user is new or returning. The JWT is generated by the jsonwebtoken library. Similar to the reason as to why we used otpLib to generate the OTP, we believe that the library provides a more reliable means to produce an encrypted string. For the usability of these tokens, the email JWT token only contains the user’s email whereas the normal JWT token contains the userId and email. |

### **Users**

### **Setting up Profile (Intended to do)**

![][image9]![][image10]

To set up a profile, the user provides three key pieces of information: a username, a user-defined property (such as a role or interest), and a profile photo. These details allow the system to automatically represent the user appropriately across different views in the application.

1\. Purpose  
Allow users to personalize their identity in the system by adding a name, role/property, and a profile photo.

 2\. User Benefit  
 Helps users differentiate themselves in multi-user or shared scenarios. Enables meaningful display in views like cards or clusters.

 3\. Technical Design  
 \- Image selected via camera or gallery  
 \- Photo uploaded to Firebase Storage; only the URL is stored in our database  
 \- Profile info stored using a PATCH request to the /edit endpoint

4\. How It Works:  
\-User inputs Name and properties, tap ‘Authenticate’.  
\-Selects profile photo from device, tap ‘upload’, then photo uploaded to Firebase Storage; download URL is saved.

 5\. Error Handling  
 \- Missing field → validation error  
 \- Unsupported image type → upload rejected  
 \- Storage error → toast notification with retry

 6\. Testing  
 \- Simulated uploads and network failures in Expo  
 \- Verified URL validity and fallback images

 7\. Design Decisions  
 \- Excluded profile fields from initial sign-in to streamline onboarding  
 \- Firebase chosen for ease of mobile integration and permission control

**Frontend**

| Topic | Explanation |
| :---: | :---: |
| UX/UI Design | Users provide three profile fields (User Name, User-defined Property, Profile Photo). These are excluded from sign-in to streamline the onboarding process. |
| Endpoint Usage | We use edit endpoints to submit or update User Name, User-defined Property, and Profile Photo. |
| Upload to Cloud Storage | After a photo is selected via the camera or gallery, the image is uploaded to Firebase Storage. The resulting file URL is returned and stored in our database. |

**Backend**

| Topic | Explanation |
| ----- | ----- |
| Picture Storage | User-uploaded photos are stored in Firebase Storage. Only the download URL is saved in our database and associated with the user profile. This approach keeps our backend lightweight and scalable. |
| Security & Access | Upload endpoints verify the user's identity. Firebase Storage Security Rules are used to restrict access to the user’s own files and to protect uploaded content from unauthorized access. |

### **Network View**

The Network View is a visual interface designed to represent entities (nodes) and their relationships (edges) in a graph layout. It provides an intuitive way for users to explore and interact with interconnected information, such as people, events, concepts, or any custom-defined data within a knowledge cluster.

![][image13]

1\. Purpose  
Provide a visual interface to explore nodes (e.g., people, concepts) and their relationships in a graph structure.

2\. User Benefit  
 nables users to see connections between information units and gain insight into how ideas or people are related.

3\. Technical Design  
 \- Force-directed graph rendering  
 \- Nodes and edges styled based on type, cluster, or tag  
 \- Interactivity: zoom/pan, drag, click for detail, hover highlight

4\. How It Works:  
\-Nodes are rendered in rows with columns based on schema.  
\-Click column headers to sort; apply filters via sidebar.  
\-Click row to open detail panel. Inline edit supported.

5\. Error Handling  
 \- Graph load failure → retry message  
 \- Unauthorized access to cluster → access denied banner

6\. Testing  
 \- Unit tests for node layout logic  
 \- UI tests for interactivity and performance under \>100 nodes

7\. Design Decisions  
 \- Considered vis.js and react-force-graph, but implemented custom D3-based layout for better control

\-Click row to open detail panel. Inline edit supported.

5\. Error Handling  
 \- Invalid field edits → error message under cell  
 \- Sort failure or API timeout → error banner

6\. Testing  
 \- Unit tests for sorting logic and schema-driven column rendering  
 \- Integration tests for edit/save cycle

7\. Design Decisions  
 \- Virtualized table to support large datasets  
 \- Chose JSON schema-based rendering for extensibility

## **Tech Stack**

**Overview**  
Our tech stack was chosen to balance rapid prototyping, cross-platform compatibility, scalability, and developer productivity. Below is the complete list and justification:

| Technology / Library | Purpose | Why We Chose It |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **TypeScript** | Strongly typed superset of JavaScript for safer, more maintainable code | Prevents type-related bugs and improves developer productivity |
| **React** | Build interactive, component-based user interfaces | Large ecosystem, strong community support, and fast development cycle |
| **React Router** | Client-side routing for React apps | Declarative API, widely adopted, integrates seamlessly with React |
| **react-hook-form** | Form handling and validation in React | Minimal re-rendering, good performance, and clean API |
| **Tailwind CSS** | Utility-first CSS framework | Speeds up styling, encourages design consistency, and integrates well with React |
| **Cytoscape.js** | Render interactive network diagrams | Powerful graph visualization capabilities, supports large datasets |
| **Zustand** | Lightweight state management for React | Minimal boilerplate, easy learning curve, good for small-to-medium state needs |
| **MiniSearch** | In-browser full-text search engine | Lightweight, no server round trips, fast for client-side search |
| **Express.js** | Backend framework for Node.js | Simple, minimalistic, and widely supported for REST APIs |
| **Better Auth** | Authentication and session management | Secure defaults, built-in provider support, reduces custom auth code |
| **SQLite** | Lightweight relational database | Simple deployment, zero-configuration, good for small-scale structured data |
| **Neo4j / DozerDB** | Graph database for relationships and network data | Flexible graph modeling; DozerDB adds multi-database support in a single instance |
| **LangChain** | Orchestration of LLM workflows | Flexible integration with multiple language models and tools |
| **Vite** | Frontend build tool and dev server | Extremely fast HMR, optimized production builds, modern ES module support |
| **Nx** | Monorepo build system and task runner | Coordinates builds for frontend, backend, and shared libraries |
| **Docker** | Containerization of services | Consistent environment between development and production |
| **Nginx** | Reverse proxy and static file server | Handles routing, SSL termination, and performance optimization |
| **Git \+ GitHub** | Version control and collaboration | Ubiquitous, integrates with CI/CD pipelines, easy collaboration |
| **Figma** | UI/UX design and prototyping | Collaborative design tool with real-time feedback capabilities |
| **Obsidian** | Developer note-taking and documentation | Markdown-based, great for organizing technical and project notes |
| **Jest** | JavaScript/TypeScript testing framework | Comprehensive testing capabilities with good TypeScript integration |
| **Prettier \+ ESLint** | Code formatting and linting | Enforces consistent style and catches potential issues early |

### **Why Not Alternative**

* **Not using React Native / Swift / Kotlin / Flutter**: Slower iteration speed and higher development workload; more platform restrictions; fewer open-source libraries; less reference material; steeper learning curve.  
* **Not using GraphQL (using REST API instead)**: Kept backend complexity low during MVP stage.

**Software Engineering Practices**

Our development process follows a set of software engineering principles and practices to ensure code quality, maintainability, and scalability. These practices guide both day-to-day development and long-term evolution of the project.

### **1\. Code Structure & Modularity**

* **Monorepo architecture** using Nx to host the frontend (`web`), backend (`api`), shared libraries, and infrastructure configuration in one repository.

* **Clear separation of concerns**:

  * `apps/` for deployable services (web client, API server)

  * `libs/` for shared types, schemas, and utilities

  * `infra/` for Dockerfiles, Compose configs, and deployment scripts

* Shared TypeScript types and schemas ensure consistent API contracts between frontend and backend.

### **2\. Version Control & Branching**

* **Git-based workflow** with `main` for stable releases and feature branches for development.

* Pull requests (PRs) are used for all changes, with mandatory code review before merge.

* Commits follow **conventional commit style** for clear history and automated changelog generation.

### **3\. Code Quality & Style**

* **TypeScript** for type safety and early error detection.

* **ESLint** and **Prettier** integrated with Nx to enforce consistent coding style.

* Lint checks and type checks are run locally before commits and in CI pipelines.

### **4\. Testing Strategy**

* **Unit tests** for core logic (e.g., form handling, search algorithms, database queries).

* **Integration tests** to validate service-to-service interactions (web ↔ API ↔ database).

* Test coverage monitored to ensure critical paths remain protected against regressions.

* Test utilities are designed for easy mocking of Neo4j, SQLite, and LangChain responses.

### **5\. Security & Authentication**

* **Better Auth** is used for secure authentication, with built-in session management and CSRF protection.

* Sensitive data never stored in the frontend or committed to the repo.

* `.env` files are environment-specific, with production secrets stored securely in deployment environments.

### **6\. Continuous Integration & Deployment**

* **CI pipelines** run linting, tests, and build steps automatically on pull requests.

* **Docker** images are built for each service (`web`, `api`) and pushed to a container registry.

* **Docker Compose** used for local dev orchestration and production deployment (multi-container with Nginx gateway).

### **7\. Documentation**

* **README** contains setup, architecture, and deployment instructions.

* Inline code comments explain complex logic, particularly around graph queries, fuzzy search, and LangChain orchestration.

* API endpoints and data contracts are documented in shared schema files.

### **8\. Development Workflow**

* Local development mirrors production as closely as possible with containerized services.

* **Hot-reload** for frontend and backend via Nx and Vite dev servers.

* Shared libraries are built automatically before dependent services during local runs.

# **Unit Testing**

## Our unit tests for the application's components have been implemented using Jest and React Testing Library. The primary focus has been verifying the proper rendering and initial mounting of each component. The tests follow a black-box methodology, concentrating specifically on ensuring components accept inputs (props, context) and render without errors or unexpected behaviors.

### **Test Methodology**

* ## Rendering Verification: Each component undergoes smoke tests that verify components render correctly without exceptions. 

* ## Mocking Dependencies: Necessary hooks and external dependencies such as navigation hooks (useRouter, usePathname) and assets (e.g., images and global CSS) are mocked to isolate the tests and prevent external factors from affecting test outcomes. 

* ## Sequential Testing: Tests are run sequentially to clearly isolate failures and ensure individual components are functioning independently. 

### **Test Outcomes**

## All unit tests have passed successfully, confirming that components:

* ## Render correctly without throwing errors. 

* ## Properly handle mocked dependencies. 

### **Example Components Tested**

* ## **`Layout`**

* ## **`Account`**

* ## **`Table`**

* ## **`Clusters Layout`**

* ## **Authentication screens (`Login`, `Signup`)** 

## The positive test outcomes indicate high reliability and stability of the UI components, ensuring a robust foundation for further development.

## **Challenges**

While building this application, we encountered several technical and workflow-related challenges:

### **1\. Debugging Complexity**

* **Multi-container setup**: Running web, API, database, and gateway containers simultaneously introduces complex networking and dependency chains. Issues can be difficult to trace because failures may stem from container configuration, environment variables, or network routing between services.

* **Distributed logs**: Debugging often requires switching between multiple log streams (`web`, `api`, `gateway`, `neo4j`) to piece together a complete picture of what went wrong.

* **Hot-reload and build caching**: In development, changes in one service (e.g., a shared TypeScript library) do not always trigger rebuilds in dependent containers, leading to stale code or inconsistent states.

### **2\. Learning Curve**

* **Technology stack breadth**: The project uses a broad range of tools and frameworks — React, Vite, React Router, react-hook-form, MiniSearch, Neo4j, SQLite, LangChain, Better Auth, Nginx, and Docker. Team members often need to learn new concepts quickly while integrating them into existing workflows.

* **Graph database concepts**: Working with Neo4j/DozerDB requires understanding Cypher queries, graph modeling, and the implications of multiple databases. This can be challenging for team members new to graph data structures.

* **Authentication library**: Adopting Better Auth reduced boilerplate, but required learning its configuration patterns, session management flow, and integration with our multi-container environment.

### **3\. Development Workflow**

**Environment configuration**: Synchronizing `.env` files and secrets across local (Windows) and production (Ubuntu ECS) environments is error-prone. Differences in file paths, Docker volume mounting, and platform-specific quirks (Windows vs. Linux) add extra steps to setup and deployment.

**Cross-platform compatibility**: Some local development workflows rely on Windows-specific paths, which must be adapted for Linux in production. This affects database volume mounting and Docker configuration.

**Integration testing**: Because many features (e.g., natural language search → Neo4j → network generation) involve multiple services, automated integration tests require careful orchestration of containers and data state.

**Performance tuning**: Balancing fast local iteration with realistic production-like conditions is tricky. Optimizations for container startup time, build caching, and API response latency often require trade-offs.

Objective: Smart Commands, Customization, Sharing & Final Polish

Week 7 (1–7 July)

* Feature 15: Smart Command Module

  * Implement Command Bar \+ LLM parsing → JSON

  * Connect to filtering, view switching, etc.

  * Add fallback search & user confirmation UI

* Feature 16: Customized Views

  * Allow users to toggle layout and save preferred column settings or color themes

Week 8 (8–14 July)

* Feature 17: Sharing Platform

  * Generate shareable view links

  * Enforce permission/expiry on backend

  * Add UI for privacy settings

* Feature 18: Export

  * Export data (visible table rows or filtered graph) to CSV/PDF

  * Add UI download link

Week 9 (15–21 July)

* Feature 19: View Personalization

  * Save/load named custom views

  * Auto-load preferred layouts on cluster entry

* Feature 20: Drag and Reposition in Network View

  * Allow user pinning of node positions

  * Store layout per user session

Week 10 (22–28 July)

* Final Testing & QA

  * Full regression testing across modules

  * Accessibility & performance pass

  * Bug fixes and polish

* Final Deliverables

  * Demo video recording

  * Final README, poster, system documentation
